name: Zane Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business economics. My week is lectures on markets and statistics, a finance seminar, and a gym session every morning at six, because I like routine. I rent a flat on Harbour Street with my cousin Dane. My dad runs a building firm, and he pays for my fees and rent, though he makes a point of saying I should earn my keep in summer, so I work on site in July and August. I use AI every day, for summaries, code, and testing business ideas.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's reselling refurbished tools to small builders, which I tested last term with a few dozen items. My dad laughed at first, then bought two drills from me at full price. My school results were average, but I'd rather learn by doing than by sitting exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, and about what I thought. I'd tell people the hype was too big, but the useful bits are real. I'd keep using the tools for my own projects, and I'd say that businesses that adapt quietly will win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things carry on, and the path is clear: finish the degree, work summers on site, grow my tool business, and maybe join my dad's firm on the money side. Pressures are ordinary, like interest rates and building costs. I'd worry a little about my average results, but my own projects help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reselling going and scale it up, maybe to a proper small shop online. I'd keep working summers on the site, since that's how I learn what builders need. I'd also put some of my earnings into shares, with a small amount each month, because I want to learn how that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ready to work. This is the world my plan was built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the shop in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell to small builders and tradespeople who don't have time to hunt for deals. I'd keep my prices fair, and I'd pay my cousin Dane to help with packing when it gets busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you didn't make money from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd call it a cheap lesson. I've lost 150 pounds so far on a bad batch, and I learned more from that than from a seminar.

say: I'd tell people the hype was too big, but the **useful** bits are real.
I'd say that businesses that adapt **quietly** will win.
think: The path is clear: finish the degree, work summers on site, and grow my **tool** business.
The pressures are ordinary: interest **rates** and building costs.
do: Scale up the **reselling** into a small online shop.
Keep working **summers** on my dad's building sites.
Put a small amount into **shares** each month.
feel: **Calm** and ready to work; this is the world my plan was built for.
S0.quote: I've lost 150 pounds so far on a bad batch, and I learned more from that than from a seminar.
fieldNote: **Adaptive** and hands-on; he learns through small, real ventures.
Sees ordinary **costs** as the main pressure, not AI.
Treats losses as **lessons**, with his dad's money as a safety net.

steps.text: Grow the refurbished tool business into a small online shop
Work summers on my dad's building sites
Put a small amount into shares every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally things are moving. People who learn the tools will do well, and people who don't will fall behind. I'd say it's no use waiting for a government to fix things, because work and effort fix more than any scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of business graduate jobs, like analysis, reporting and admin, will shrink. That's a risk for me, with my average results. But I'm already using these tools every day, so I'd have an edge over classmates who are slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build more of my own business, using the tools to run it with almost no staff. I'd go for a placement at a firm that uses AI heavily, to learn it from inside. I'd also ask my dad whether I could handle estimating and ordering for his firm, as a test. It would show I'm useful in the real world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit impatient. I'd like to move faster than the world does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about people who can't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they should learn a trade or a skill. Apprenticeships are underrated. But I'd also help my cousin Dane, who's slower with tech, and show him how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, with training. But I don't want handouts. If I'm helped, I'd want it to be short-term and linked to work.

Offer to handle **estimating** and ordering for my dad's firm.

fieldNote: Frames the change as an **opportunity** while admitting the grad job risk.

Plans to **help** his cousin, showing loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people should be honest about it. Two years is fast, and no one has a plan. I'd say families and businesses should look after their own, and the government should stay out of the way, but also not let people starve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy and focused. My degree would be about worthless, since economics is thinking work. But my own skills, which are the tools and the selling, are the kind that might be the last to go. And my dad's firm is hands-on until about 2031, which gives us some breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my effort to things that last: my own business, relationships and physical work. I'd work extra on my dad's building sites to learn trades, like tiling or electrical basics. I'd save everything I can and invest a part in assets that could hold value, like tools and equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with adrenaline. It's like the start of a race I didn't sign up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, because dropping out for a prediction is a big call. But I'd stop treating it as the main thing and work on the other stuff in the evenings and summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years change your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the long game. With two years you pick what's in front of you: the business, the site and the money.

I'd say families and businesses should look after their **own**.

fieldNote: Turns the threat into **practical** work: trades, savings, assets.

steps.text: Learn tiling and basic electrical work on my dad's sites

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. I'd tell friends to learn the tools, learn a trade and build savings. I'd say it's good to be uncomfortable now, so you aren't surprised later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about my position. By 2031 I'd be 23, with a business, a degree and some site skills. The thinking jobs may be gone, but I'd be self-employed, and my dad's firm might still need people until 2034 for the hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, grow the tool business into something bigger, and work summers on site. I'd invest regularly, and put money into a small property or equipment with my dad's help. I'd also look into a short apprenticeship or a licence, like a safety or estimating certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, and a little restless. Five years feels like enough time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers disappear because of an economic shock, or the tools get so good that anyone can run a business like mine. Then I'd lose my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move toward the physical side, like running crews or equipment hire, where you still need people and places.

I'd tell friends to learn the tools, learn a **trade** and build savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and that people should keep working and building. I'd tell friends not to panic and to keep doing something real. There's no reason to stop planning for a family, a house or a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a few years of business behind me and maybe a family. Machines might do most of the office work, but I'd already be an owner, not an employee. That's the safest place to be in any version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and build my business steadily. I'd take on a small team of two or three. I'd learn the new tools every year, and I'd invest in property over time. I'd also keep helping my dad's firm, because family and work go together for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud. Ten years is a good run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your life to look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, a wife, a couple of kids and a business that pays for it all. Church on Sunday and work on Monday. I want to keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if AGI makes all that impossible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd adjust, since I'm good at that. But I wouldn't give up on a plan just because someone predicts it will fail.

I'd say there's no reason to stop planning for a family, a house or a **business**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years leaves no time to build up an asset or a skill. What would help is honest information about which jobs and businesses last, and quick training in practical skills, like trades, not just courses on a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I feel lucky I have family who can back me, and I'd like to see people without that get the chance to learn by doing too.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn by doing than by sitting exams.
portrait: Zane is an 18-year-old **business** economics student who uses AI every day and resells refurbished tools to small builders.
His dad's building firm pays his fees and rent, and he works summers on **site** to earn his keep.
He is traditional and free-market: work, family, church and ownership matter more than **schemes** or handouts.
He stays calm in most worlds and turns only **uneasy** at two years, when his degree could be worth little.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most, because two years leaves no time to build assets or skills.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information** about which jobs and businesses last, plus fast, practical training in trades.
